a: a local attribution explains the output, not the system's role in the procedure
b: attribution methods are defined for neural networks only, not for tree ensembles
c: feature attributions are trade secrets that cannot lawfully be disclosed outside
d: the explanation must be produced by a notified body rather than by the deployer
explain: Art 86 asks for a clear and meaningful account of the role the system played in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision, in terms the person can act on. A saliency chart may feed into that, but it answers a different question.

sources.quote: shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

q: A caseworker may override the model's recommendation but approves 99% of them within three seconds. The core failure is:
a: automation bias: oversight that is nominal, which the design itself must counter
b: insufficient accuracy, which is why the caseworker finds nothing left to correct
c: a record-keeping breach, three seconds leaving no usable audit trail behind it
d: absence of CE marking, without which the system should not be in operation at all
explain: Art 14(4)(b) expressly requires oversight measures that keep the person aware of the tendency to over-rely on outputs, particularly where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions to be taken by natural persons. Rubber-stamping means the measure exists on paper but is not effective, which is what Art 14 demands.

sources.quote: to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias), in particular for high-risk AI systems used to provide information or recommendations for decisions to be taken by natural persons;
that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.

q: A large public administration is implementing Art 4 across 20 000 staff. The approach that best fits the obligation is:
a: role-differentiated measures, from awareness for users to deeper training for overseers
b: one mandatory e-learning module for all staff, repeated annually and tracked centrally
c: certification of the organisation against an AI management system standard covering skills
d: publication of an internal register of AI systems with owners and risk classifications
explain: Art 4 requires measures that take account of technical knowledge, experience, education and training, and of the context in which the systems are used, so proportionality by role is the whole point. A single uniform course ignores that, and a management-system certificate evidences process rather than literacy.

sources.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in
This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

q: A border agency runs face matching at a single global decision threshold. The most serious fairness problem is:
a: false-match and false-non-match rates diverge across groups at a fixed threshold
b: matching latency will differ measurably across demographic groups at that threshold
c: global thresholds are among the practices prohibited outright by Art 5 of the Act
d: facial embeddings become biometric data only once a match above threshold returns
explain: Demographic differentials in error rates at a fixed operating point are the documented failure mode in face recognition testing, and they distribute the burden of errors unequally. Nothing in Art 5 bans a global threshold as such: biometric identification at a border is high-risk, not prohibited.

sources.quote: Technical inaccuracies of AI systems intended for the remote biometric identification of natural persons can lead to biased results and entail discriminatory effects. The risk of such biased results and discriminatory effects is particularly relevant with regard to age, ethnicity, race, sex or disabilities.
in the context of migration, asylum or border control management, for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons, with the exception of the verification of travel documents.
Publicly accessible spaces should not include prisons or border control.

q: An AI governance lead already holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification and now needs a process for identifying and treating AI-specific risks. The natural companion document is:
a: ISO/IEC 23894, guidance on AI risk management aligned with ISO 31000
b: ISO/IEC 27001, the requirements standard for information security management
c: ISO/IEC 42005, which covers records of processing for machine-learning models
d: ISO 9001, the generic quality management requirements standard for suppliers
explain: ISO/IEC 23894 gives AI-specific risk management guidance built on the ISO 31000 structure and is designed to sit under an ISO/IEC 42001 management system. ISO/IEC 42005 exists but concerns AI system impact assessment, not records of processing, which is what makes it a convincing wrong answer.

q: In a three-lines model applied to AI governance, validating a deployed model and challenging the owning team's risk assessment belongs to:
a: the second line, the risk and compliance function providing expertise, monitoring and challenge
b: the first line, the business unit that owns and runs the model
c: the third line, internal audit reporting to the audit committee
d: an external notified body appointed under the AI Act procedures
explain: In the IIA Three Lines Model, second-line roles provide expertise, support, monitoring and challenge to the first line and are part of management, not fully independent of it. Independent, objective assurance is the third line (internal audit), which audits whether the validation process works rather than doing the validation. Notified bodies assess conformity of certain high-risk systems, a different exercise.

q: A group discovers 140 AI uses across its business units, none of them centrally recorded. The first governance control to put in place is:
a: an AI inventory recording owner, purpose, risk tier and data for each use
b: a board-approved risk appetite statement with quantitative tolerance limits
c: a mandatory approval gate blocking every new AI project until it is reviewed
d: an annual independent audit of the highest-risk systems in the AI portfolio
explain: You cannot classify, assign ownership or assess risk against systems you have not enumerated, and both the Art 26 deployer duties and the Art 27 FRIA presuppose knowing which systems you run. Risk appetite and approval gates are sound next steps, but they operate on an inventory.

sources.quote: GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.

q: A city deploys an Annex III system to allocate social housing. Which assessment obligation applies?
a: both a data protection impact assessment and a fundamental rights assessment
b: a fundamental rights impact assessment only, which absorbs the data protection one
c: a data protection impact assessment only, the city not being a private operator
d: neither, both duties falling on the provider that placed the system on the market
explain: The city is a body governed by public law deploying an Annex III system, so Art 27 applies, while a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects triggers GDPR Art 35. Art 27(4), as amended, lets the FRIA cross-reference or reuse parts of an existing DPIA, but it does not replace it.

sources.quote: deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III, shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights

a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person
include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment or include relevant parts thereof in the fundamental rights impact assessment.

social security benefits, social services providing protection in cases such as maternity, illness, industrial accidents, dependency or old age and loss of employment and social and housing assistance

q: A Union agency deploys a high-risk AI system for staff selection. Which body acts as its market surveillance authority?
a: the European Data Protection Supervisor, for Union bodies in the Act's scope
b: the market surveillance authority of the Member State hosting the agency's seat
c: the AI Office, which supervises all AI used by the Union's own administration
d: the European Ombudsman, on complaint by an affected candidate or staff member
explain: Art 74 designates the EDPS as market surveillance authority for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the Act, excluding the Court of Justice acting in its judicial capacity. The EDPS also holds the power to fine Union bodies under Art 100, so supervision and sanction sit in the same hands.

sources.quote: Where Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies fall within the scope of this Regulation, the European Data Protection Supervisor shall act as their market surveillance authority, except in relation to the Court of Justice of the European Union acting in its judicial capacity.
The European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of this Regulation.

q: A Commission official wants to paste a draft internal note into a publicly available chatbot to tighten the wording. Under the Commission's staff guidelines on online generative AI tools this is:
a: not allowed, as only information already in the public domain may be entered
b: allowed, provided the output is not copied verbatim into any public document
c: allowed, provided the note carries no personal data of identifiable individuals
d: not allowed, staff being barred from using such tools for any work purpose at all
explain: The guidelines bar staff from entering any non-public information or personal data into publicly available generative AI tools, and separately forbid reproducing outputs verbatim in public documents. Stripping out personal data is not enough, because the confidentiality restriction is wider than data protection, and the tools are not banned outright.

q: Twelve months after deployment, a provider sees its high-risk system's precision fall as the client population shifts. The Act addresses this through:
a: Art 72, the post-market monitoring system and plan the provider runs
b: Art 61, which governs informed consent for testing in real-world conditions
c: Art 43, requiring a fresh conformity assessment every twelve months of use
d: Art 17, the quality management system the notified body re-audits each year
explain: Art 72 obliges providers to collect and analyse performance data across the system's lifetime under a documented plan, feeding the Art 9 risk management process and triggering corrective action under Art 20. A substantial modification would require reassessment, but ordinary drift is monitored, not re-certified on a calendar.

sources.quote: The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime
The post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV.

q: A ministry signs a five-year contract for a model-backed document service. Which clause does most to limit lock-in?
a: version pinning with notice, and export of prompts, data and tuning artefacts
b: a service credit regime tied to monthly availability and response-time targets
c: a most-favoured-customer pricing clause benchmarked against comparable buyers
d: a commitment that the supplier will not train on the ministry's data or outputs
explain: Exit cost is driven by whether the buyer can leave with the assets that make the service work, and by protection against silent model changes mid-term. Availability credits, pricing benchmarks and no-training commitments are all worth having, but none of them makes switching supplier feasible.

q: An audit shows a screening model is well calibrated within each group but has unequal false-negative rates between them. The correct reading is:
a: calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold when base rates differ
b: the model is biased and recalibrating it per group will equalise the error rates
c: calibration within groups is the accepted legal definition of fairness in the Union
d: unequal false-negative rates always indicate that a protected attribute was used
explain: This is the impossibility result: where base rates differ, a classifier cannot simultaneously be calibrated within groups and equalised on false-positive and false-negative rates, so choosing a criterion is a judgement about which harm matters more. Neither recalibration nor dropping the protected attribute dissolves the trade-off.
